tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

action.description: What to do. 'attach' opens the live simulator panel for the user — call it BEFORE you build or launch, as soon as the user wants to see the app: on a booted simulator it opens immediately, and otherwise it returns a clear, harmless error (boot or build first, then retry it). Do not skip the early attach because 'launch' also attaches — the panel should be open before the build starts. The panel is the user's view, not a precondition — 'screenshot' and input actions work without it. Skip it only when the user has no interest in watching; 'launch' installs and launches an .app (it also re-attaches, but call 'attach' early rather than relying on that); 'screenshot' returns a PNG of the current screen; 'inspect' returns the accessibility tree of the front app (what a screen reader reads, which can differ from what is drawn) as JSON — per element: type, label, value, frame [x,y,width,height] in device points from the top-left, traits the type does not imply, enabled only when false, children. Prefer it to 'screenshot' to find what to tap (tap a frame's center), read text, or check a control's state or value; use 'screenshot' for layout, color, and images. Default: the whole visible tree; x/y: the element under that point with its descendants (a point between controls hits their container); marker: the first element whose label (or match_key) contains that text. Hidden, off-screen, and illegibly small elements are omitted and counted, and text longer than its area shows is cut and ends with ... (occlusion and transparency are not detected); a tree over the size cap loses its deepest levels first and says so — narrow with x/y or marker; 'tap'/'swipe'/'text'/'button' inject input; 'touch_path' performs a single-finger drag along an arbitrary path (eased curves, long-press-then-drag); 'touch2_path' is the two-finger variant for pinch/rotate; 'open_url' opens a deep link; 'detach' closes the panel/stream. NOTE: a 'swipe' or 'touch_path' whose start point is on-screen and within 4pt of an edge performs the OS edge gesture instead of a plain drag — left=back, top=notification shade, bottom=home/app-switcher, right=Control Center (mapped to the current interface orientation). Start more than 4pt from the edge to drag or scroll content near the bezel.

app_path.description: For 'launch': path to the built .app bundle (e.g. DerivedData/.../Build/Products/Debug-iphonesimulator/MyApp.app).

device.description: Simulator name (e.g. 'iPhone 17 Pro') or UDID. Defaults to the currently attached simulator, or the first booted one. The first use of a device asks the user for permission.

udid.description: Alias for 'device' (identical semantics: simulator name or UDID). Pass at most one of 'device' / 'udid'.

bundle_id.description: For 'launch': bundle identifier. If omitted, extracted from the .app's Info.plist.

points.description: For 'touch_path': touch path samples in device points. First point is touch-down; last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000, total clamped to 30s).

points2.description: For 'touch2_path': two-finger path samples in device points. Each sample carries both contacts (x1/y1, x2/y2); first is touch-down, last is touch-up. dt_ms is the delay before that sample (0-1000, total clamped to 30s).

duration.description: Seconds. For 'tap', >0.5 is a long-press. For 'swipe', the gesture duration (default 0.3).

url.description: For 'open_url': URL or scheme to open in the simulator.

marker.description: For 'inspect': return only the first element (tree order, with its descendants) whose match_key attribute contains this case-sensitive substring. Omit for the whole tree, or pass x/y instead for the element under a point.

match_key.description: For 'inspect' with 'marker': the attribute to match — label (default), value, or role (the element type).

entries.description:
Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead. Exception: claude.ai artifact links (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}) ARE fetchable via your claude.ai login — use WebFetch, not curl (curl gets the SPA shell or a Cloudflare 403).

content.text:
The scenario is mostly accurate, but it gets two details wrong: the `usage` field, and what the search looks at. It also leaves open several things the current docs settle. I checked it against Anthropic's tool search page (platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/tool-search-tool). One framing issue matters too: this is how the **raw Claude API** works, and this Claude Code session uses a different mechanism for its deferred Gmail tools.

## Wrong

- **The `usage` block in response #1.** The docs say tool search "isn't metered as a separate server tool". `usage.server_tool_use` has no tool search field, so `tool_search_requests: 1` shouldn't be there. The tool definitions that the search loads are billed as ordinary input tokens.
- **Step 5, what gets searched.** Both the BM25 and regex search variants look at tool names, descriptions, **argument names, and argument descriptions**, not just names and descriptions.

## Uncertain in the draft, now confirmed

- **Block and field names** are exactly as written: `server_tool_use`, `tool_search_tool_result`, the nested `tool_search_tool_search_result`, and `tool_references: [{"type": "tool_reference", "tool_name": ...}]`. The BM25 input field is `query`; the regex variant uses `pattern`.
- **Step 11, re-expansion on later turns** is documented, not just inferred: "The API expands `tool_reference` blocks throughout the conversation history, so Claude can reuse discovered tools in later turns without re-searching." You must send the assistant blocks back unchanged along with the same `tools` array. Never send a `tool_result` for the `srvtoolu_...` ID, because the API rejects the request.
- **Steps 3, 6 and 7** match the docs almost word for word. Deferred tools stay out of the system-prompt prefix, a `tool_reference` is added inline, and the API expands it, so the prompt cache survives.

## Worth adding

- **Result count:** a search returns up to 5 matches by default. The model can pass a `limit` from 1 to 10,000 in its search input.
- **No beta header:** the docs' quick-start curl sends none. The last bullet's "with the beta enabled" is stale for the Claude API itself.
- **Step 4, how the model knows to search:** the docs don't publish the search tool's built-in description. They do tell hosts to add a system-prompt line such as "You can search for tools to interact with Slack, GitHub, and Jira." So a host-supplied hint is the expected pattern, not a guess.
- **Steps 1–2:** MCP's `tools/list` returns `inputSchema` in camelCase. The host has to rename it to `input_schema` when building the API request.
- **Other constraints:** a deferred tool can't also carry `cache_control` (that's a 400 error). At least one tool, normally the search tool, must stay non-deferred. A search with no matches returns an empty `tool_references` array, not an error.
- **API-side MCP:** if the API connects to the MCP server itself (Anthropic's "MCP connector"), you don't mark individual tools. You set `defer_loading` once in `default_config` on the `mcp_toolset` entry.

## Framing: this session doesn't use that mechanism

The 23 Gmail tools deferred in this Claude Code session are loaded differently:
- Claude Code lists the deferred tools by name only, in a system message.
- I get their schemas through a regular client-side tool called `ToolSearch`, which runs inside Claude Code, not on Anthropic's servers.
- `ToolSearch` returns the full schemas as text in an ordinary tool result.

The docs describe a "custom tool search" path where a client tool returns `tool_reference` blocks in a normal `tool_result` and the API expands them. I can't tell whether Claude Code uses that path underneath or injects the schema text directly, because I only see what reaches my context.

If this write-up is meant to explain what happened in this chat, add a note that it describes the raw API. If it's meant as API documentation, fixing the `usage` block and step 5 is enough. The page has no captured response for BM25 specifically. One real request would confirm the exact JSON.

content.text:
I have five tools from the JusPrin MCP server, which runs inside the JusPrin app. One reads the open project. The other four read and change process settings, the print settings such as layer height, walls and infill. I just loaded their full schemas, and I haven't called any of them.

| Tool | What it does | Inputs |
|---|---|---|
| `workspace_inspect` | Returns a summary of the open project: plates, objects, preset names, selection IDs and undo history. It returns no setting values. Its IDs only work within the `sessionId` it returns. | none |
| `settings_search` | Finds process settings by key, label or description, one page at a time. A single page is not the full list of settings you can change. | `query`, optional `limit` (up to 25) and `cursor` |
| `settings_get` | Reads current values and which preset each one comes from. The server says to call it before proposing a change. | `keys` (1–32) |
| `settings_preview_patch` | Checks a set of changes without applying them. Returns a `sessionId` and `revision`. | `changes`: a map of key to value, 1–32 entries |
| `settings_apply_patch` | Applies the changes as one all-or-nothing edit. | `changes`, `expectedSessionId` and `expectedRevision` from a fresh preview, optional `intent` |

The four settings tools only work when the active process preset is for FFF (ordinary filament) printing.

The server's instructions describe this order:
1. Inspect the project, then search for or read the settings you need.
2. Preview the change.
3. Apply it using the `sessionId` and `revision` from that preview. The apply call blocks until someone approves it in the JusPrin Agent panel.
4. If apply fails with `stale_workspace` (the project changed since the preview), read and preview again.

Two cautions:
- **Undo:** the project's Undo does not reverse a settings change. To roll one back, revert the preset or apply the opposite changes.
- **`workspace_unavailable` error:** JusPrin isn't running or has no project open.

The `intent` field on apply should be what the user asked for, in their own words, in 40 characters or fewer. It should not be a description of which settings changed.

intent.description: What the user asked this setup to be, in their own words, as one line of at most 40 characters. Not a description of the settings you changed. Send it whenever the change came from something the user asked for.

entries.description: Read a bounded summary of the open project, plates and objects, setup names, selection IDs, and native history. IDs are strings scoped to the returned sessionId. No process-setting values are exposed by this tool.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about Claude Code MCP tool search and ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH:

## Overview

MCP Tool Search is a Claude Code capability that enables dynamic tool discovery. Instead of loading all tool definitions into context upfront, Claude searches for and loads only the tools it needs.

## Deferred Tools

Tool search keeps MCP context usage low by deferring tool definitions until Claude needs them. Only tool names and server instructions load at session start, and full schemas are fetched on demand. As of Claude Code v2.1.69, all built-in system tools (Bash, Read, Edit, Write, Glob, Grep, Agent, etc.) are deferred behind ToolSearch — the same mechanism previously used only for MCP tools.

## ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH Configuration

Leave it unset for the default, where all MCP tools are deferred. Set it to true to force deferral through a proxy, false to load everything upfront, or auto to load definitions upfront while they total under 10 percent of the context window. Use auto:N for a custom percentage, such as auto:5.

## Always-Loaded Tools

Mark a server's tools as always visible with alwaysLoad in its .mcp.json entry, and every tool from that server then loads at session start regardless of ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH.

## Known Issues

HTTP/Streamable HTTP MCP tools should be deferred behind ToolSearch the same way stdio MCP tools are. This is an open bug where HTTP-based MCP tools aren't being deferred as efficiently as stdio tools.

content.content:
# Advanced Tool Use on Claude Developer Platform (Nov 24, 2025)

## (1) Why Tool Search Exists

**Problem Statement:**
"That's 58 tools consuming approximately 55K tokens before the conversation even starts."

Token consumption concerns: Five MCP servers alone could consume ~55K tokens, with potential for 100K+ overhead when adding services like Jira (~17K tokens).

**Accuracy Issues:**
"The most common failures are wrong tool selection and incorrect parameters, especially when tools have similar names like `notification-send-user` vs. `notification-send-channel`."

**Performance Improvements:**
"Opus 4 improved from 49% to 74%, and Opus 4.5 improved from 79.5% to 88.1% with Tool Search Tool enabled."

## (2) Search Variants

The post mentions "The Claude Developer Platform provides regex-based and BM25-based search tools out of the box, but you can also implement custom search tools using embeddings or other strategies."

No detailed explanation distinguishes why both server-side variants exist or compares them to client-side approaches.

## (3) Claude Code & Tool Search/MCP

The post states: "Claude for Excel uses Programmatic Tool Calling to read and modify spreadsheets with thousands of rows without overloading the model's context window."

No mention of Claude Code using Tool Search or MCP tool search specifically.

## (4) Prompt Caching Interaction

"Tool Search Tool doesn't break prompt caching because deferred tools are excluded from the initial prompt entirely. They're only added to context after Claude searches for them, so your system prompt and core tool definitions remain cacheable."

## (5) Tradeoffs & When Not to Use

**Use it when:**
"Tool definitions consuming >10K tokens; Experiencing tool selection accuracy issues; Building MCP-powered systems with multiple servers; 10+ tools available"

**Less beneficial when:**
"Small tool library (<10 tools); All tools used frequently in every session; Tool definitions are compact"

content.text:
Anthropic gives a one-line reason for offering both, and no reason for which one Claude Code uses. It's also less complicated than two separate systems. There is one loading mechanism (mark tools `defer_loading: true`, then return `tool_reference` blocks that the API expands into full definitions) and two ways to produce the references.

## What Anthropic actually says

- **Built-in search** runs on Anthropic's servers and comes in regex and BM25 variants. The engineering post calls these tools that work "out of the box". You just add the search tool to the request.
- **Custom search** exists so you can use "search methods the built-in variants don't provide, such as embedding-based retrieval". That sentence is the whole justification in the API docs. The post says the same: you "can also implement custom search tools using embeddings or other strategies."
- **Why tool search exists at all.** Tool definitions use up context: five MCP servers came to 58 tools and about 55K tokens. Picking the right tool also gets harder as the list grows. Anthropic reports accuracy rising from 49% to 74% on Opus 4 and from 79.5% to 88.1% on Opus 4.5 with tool search on.
- **The cost of the client-side path.** Claude Code's docs admit it: "Tool search adds one extra round-trip each time Claude searches for tools." They argue the smaller context on every turn makes up for it.

## What they don't say

None of the pages I read explains why Claude Code runs its own `ToolSearch` instead of the built-in server-side tool. The following are **my inferences** from documented behavior, not reasons Anthropic has given:

1. **Exact-name loading.** Claude Code gives the model a list of all deferred tool names up front, so the model can load tools by name with `select:`. The built-in tools only rank by regex or BM25 over the tool definitions.
2. **Waiting for slow MCP servers.** The Claude Code MCP docs say that when a needed server is "still connecting in the background," the wait "happens inside the `ToolSearch` call." A search that runs locally can wait for a local connection. A search on Anthropic's servers can only see the tools in the request it was sent.
3. **One code path for everything.** Claude Code also defers some of its own built-in tools, not just MCP tools. It also falls back to loading everything up front where tool search isn't supported: most third-party proxies (the docs say they "don't forward `tool_reference` blocks"), Azure-hosted Foundry deployments, and older models on Google Cloud. Owning the search step makes those switches easier, though the docs don't say that was the motive.

If you want an authoritative answer, the likely places are the claude-code GitHub issues or an Anthropic staff reply. I haven't found either.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about OpenAI's Responses API tool search, defer_loading, and deferred tools:

## Overview

Tool search allows the model to dynamically search for and load tools into the model's context as needed, which helps avoid loading all tool definitions into the model's context up front and may help reduce overall token usage and cost.

## Key Components

**Tool Search:** To activate tool search in the Responses API, you must add tool_search as a tool in your tools array.

**Defer Loading:** If you are using functions, mark the ones you want to defer with defer_loading: true. When you defer a tool, the model doesn't load its full definition into the context until it decides that it needs the tool. The model then uses tool search to load the relevant tools before it calls them.

## Two Approaches

Hosted tool search: OpenAI searches across the deferred tools you declared in the request and returns the loaded subset in the same response. Client-executed tool search: The model emits a tool_search_call, your application performs the lookup, and you return a matching tool_search_output.

## Model Support

In the Responses API, only gpt-5.4 and later models support tool_search.

## Benefits

For optimal cost and latency, tool search is designed to preserve the model's cache. When new tools are discovered by the model, they are injected at the end of the context window.

content.content:
# Tool Search: Essential Reference

## Tool Search Definition
The `tool_search` tool enables dynamic loading: `{"type": "tool_search"}` activates the feature in the Responses API for `gpt-5.4` and later models.

## Defer Loading Placement
Set `"defer_loading": true` on:
- Individual functions within namespaces
- Functions at the root level
- MCP server tool definitions

The flag applies to function contents, not the namespace object itself.

## Execution Modes

**Hosted mode** (`execution: "server"` or omitted):
- API searches deferred tools you declared upfront
- Returns `tool_search_call` and `tool_search_output` items in one response

**Client mode** (`execution: "client"`):
- Model emits `tool_search_call` with search arguments
- Your application performs discovery
- You return `tool_search_output` with loaded tools in next request

## What the Model Sees Initially
- Namespace/MCP server names and descriptions only
- Individual deferred function names and descriptions (parameter schemas deferred)
- Non-deferred function full definitions

## Multi-turn Behavior
Pass previous response items back using `toResponseInputItems()` helper or manual round-tripping. Include the `tool_search_output` item with matched `call_id`. Tools loaded remain callable in subsequent turns without reloading.

## Caching Impact
"All tools are loaded at the end of the model's context window...This allows the model's cache to be preserved from one request to another, lowering overall costs and boosting speed."

## Key Limitation
"For maximum token savings, we recommend grouping deferred functions into namespaces or MCP servers...aim to keep each namespace to fewer than 10 functions for better token efficiency and model performance."

content.text:
Yes. OpenAI's Responses API has the same feature, with the same flag name. You add `{"type": "tool_search"}` to `tools` and set `defer_loading: true` on the functions you want kept out of context until needed. Only `gpt-5.4` and later models support it.

**How it compares with Anthropic's version:**

| | OpenAI Responses API | Anthropic Messages API |
|---|---|---|
| Turn it on | a `tool_search` tool plus `defer_loading: true` | a `tool_search_tool_regex_*` or `_bm25_*` tool plus `defer_loading: true` |
| Search runs on the provider's servers | `execution: "server"`, the default | the built-in regex or BM25 variants |
| Search runs in your app | `execution: "client"`: the model emits a `tool_search_call`, and your app replies with a `tool_search_output` in the next request | a custom tool of your own that returns `tool_reference` blocks in an ordinary `tool_result` |
| What the model sees up front | names and descriptions of deferred functions, plus names and descriptions of namespaces and MCP servers; parameter schemas are held back | only the search tool and non-deferred tools; the host has to add any hint about what can be searched |
| Where `defer_loading` goes | root-level functions, functions inside a namespace, MCP server tool definitions | individual tools, or `default_config` on an `mcp_toolset` |
| Later turns | send the earlier items back; loaded tools stay callable | send the history back; the API expands references again |
| Caching | discovered tools are added at the end of the context, so the cache survives | `tool_reference` blocks are added inline, so the cached prefix survives |

**Two design differences worth noting:**
- **Client-side search is a first-class feature at OpenAI.** It has its own item types, while Anthropic reuses a plain `tool_result`. Adding client mode fills the gap the previous answer described: the provider can't wait on a server that only your app can see.
- **OpenAI groups tools into namespaces.** It recommends putting deferred functions in namespaces or MCP servers with fewer than 10 functions each, so the model sees one short description per group instead of every tool.

**Not verified:** the fetch tool summarized OpenAI's page instead of returning it verbatim, so I haven't seen the exact JSON for `tool_search_call` and `tool_search_output`. In particular, I can't tell whether client mode returns full tool definitions or references to them.

- Ask what JusPrin tools exist, which should trigger a tool search.

## What the checks showed

- **JusPrin's MCP server is local.** Claude Code launches it as a subprocess over stdio (the `jusprin-mcp` binary in the RelWithDebInfo build). OpenAI's hosted MCP tool connects to a server by URL from OpenAI's side, so it can't reach this one. Something on this Mac has to connect to JusPrin and present its tools to OpenAI as deferred functions, the way Claude Code does.
- **No `OPENAI_API_KEY` is set** in my shell.
- **The Python `openai` package isn't installed.** Node is available.
- **OpenAI's Codex CLI is installed** at `/opt/homebrew/bin/codex`. It's OpenAI's counterpart to Claude Code and can launch stdio MCP servers.

## Your decision: which program talks to OpenAI

**A. My own small script (recommended).** A Node script of about 150 lines in the scratchpad would:
- launch `jusprin-mcp` with the same arguments Claude Code uses;
- send its five tools to the Responses API with `defer_loading: true`, plus `{"type": "tool_search"}`;
- run the same three user turns;
- log every raw HTTP request and response body.

That closes the gap we couldn't close in Claude Code, which never logs the wire request. It can also run the whole thing twice, once with OpenAI running the search (`execution: "server"`) and once with the script running it (`execution: "client"`).

**B. Codex CLI.** This is the more literal copy: OpenAI's own agent, like Claude Code is Anthropic's, and it would show which search mode OpenAI chose for its own product. The evidence would again be indirect: Codex's session files, logs and binary, like before. My hypothesis is that Codex doesn't log raw HTTP bodies either; I haven't checked.

Running both is also reasonable: A for how the API behaves, B for what OpenAI's product does.

content.text:
I've finished the measurements and am writing up the results. Everything below comes from the logged request and response bodies and OpenAI's token-counting endpoint.

The experiment ran end to end in both of OpenAI's search modes, and the tool loading works quite differently from Anthropic's version. With OpenAI running the search (hosted mode), the model loaded the whole `jusprin` namespace in turn 1 by name. The loaded result contains full tool definitions, and the client resends them with the history on every later turn. With my script running the search (client mode), the model couldn't see JusPrin at all until turn 3, and it searched only when it needed a tool.

## What each run did

Same three questions as the Claude Code session, `gpt-5.4`, full history resent each turn (`store: false`).

**Hosted search (4 API calls)**

| Turn | Model output | Input tokens |
|---|---|---|
| "what's the jusprin mcp tools…" | `tool_search_call` with arguments `{"paths": ["jusprin"]}`, then `tool_search_output` holding the full `jusprin` namespace with all five definitions, then its answer, **all in one response** | 1,068 |
| "all of them deferred?" | answer only | 1,351 |
| "what's on my jusprin workspace?" | `function_call: workspace_inspect` with `namespace: "jusprin"` and no new search; then, after the MCP result, the answer | 1,490 → 1,705 |

**Client search (5 API calls)**

| Turn | Model output | Input tokens |
|---|---|---|
| "what's the jusprin mcp tools…" | answer only: it said it could see only `tool_search.tool` and `multi_tool_use.parallel`, and no JusPrin tools | 161 |
| "all of them deferred?" | answer only: they "appear to be deferred" | 307 |
| "what's on my jusprin workspace?" | `tool_search_call` with `{"goal": "Discover JusPrin workspace inspection tools…"}`. My script returned all five definitions. Next call: `function_call: workspace_inspect`. Then the answer. | 427 → 1,071 → 1,288 |

Both runs reported the same workspace, a project called `3x3_cali_rl_MINI` with one object, so the MCP calls worked. That's a different project from the empty "Untitled" one Claude Code saw earlier, so the workspace changed in between.

## What the model sees before any search

Token counts for the same first request, from OpenAI's free input-token counting endpoint:

| Tool setup | Input tokens |
|---|---|
| no tools | 107 |
| JusPrin tools not deferred | 530 (346 with empty parameter schemas) |
| hosted search, deferred tools in a namespace | 497; unchanged when I pad every function description or empty every parameter schema; **646** when I pad only the namespace description |
| hosted search, deferred tools at the root (no namespace) | 739; **1,539** when I pad the function descriptions |
| client search, with or without the deferred tools | 161 either way |
| hosted search with no deferred tools | 400 error: "tools.tool_search requires at least one deferred tool" |

So up front:
- **Hosted search, namespaced tools:** the model sees the namespace's name and description, but no function descriptions and no parameter schemas.
- **Hosted search, root-level tools:** the function descriptions are sent up front. That costs more tokens here than not deferring at all (739 vs 530). I didn't test whether root-level parameter schemas are sent too.
- **Client search:** the model sees nothing about the deferred tools. As in Claude Code, the host has to tell the model what can be searched.

## Compared with the Claude Code experiment

| | Claude Code with Anthropic | OpenAI hosted search | OpenAI client search |
|---|---|---|---|
| Who runs the search | Claude Code (a normal tool) | OpenAI, inside the same response | my script |
| API calls for search plus one tool call | 3 (search, result, then the call) | 2 | 3 |
| How the model asks | exact names via `select:` | a namespace path | a free-text `goal` |
| What goes into the history | `tool_reference` blocks (names only), which the API expands on every request | **full definitions** in `tool_search_output`, resent by the client | **full definitions**, supplied by the client |
| What the model knows up front | all 243 deferred names, from a Claude Code attachment | namespace name and description | nothing |
| Loaded tools reused on a later turn without searching again | yes | yes | yes (only one turn tested) |

## Other things I ran into

- **Client mode requires the search tool to have a `description`.** My first client run failed with a 400 error until I added one. The docs didn't mention this.
- **Odd `namespace` value in client mode.** My script returned bare functions, not wrapped in a namespace, and the model's call came back with `namespace: "workspace_inspect"`, the tool's own name. The call still worked.
- **Caching wasn't tested.** Every response reported 0 cached tokens. OpenAI only caches prompts of 1,024 tokens or more, and most of these requests were shorter, so the zeros don't show that caching fails.
- **The second question isn't a fair repeat.** "all of them deferred?" relied on context from the Claude Code conversation. Without that context, the hosted-mode model read "deferred" as "waits for approval". That's a difference in how the model understood the question, not in the mechanism.

## Limits

- Each mode ran once, so the model's choices (when to search, what to ask for) could vary between runs.
- I only tested sending the full history back (`store: false`). I didn't test OpenAI's server-side conversation state (`previous_response_id`).
- I didn't calculate cost. Total usage was about 5,600 input and 600 output tokens for hosted mode, and 3,300 input and 470 output tokens for client mode.
- My client-mode search is a crude keyword match. Here it returned all five tools.

Files are in the scratchpad (`/private/tmp/claude/claude-502/-Users-kenneth-Projects-JusPrin/dbaa3011-c233-4f2d-a740-f723f6e5dfaf/scratchpad/openai-toolsearch/`):
- `run.mjs`: the experiment script
- `count.mjs` and `count2.mjs`: the token counts
- `logs/server-2026-09-15T19-25-31-841Z/` and `logs/client-2026-09-15T19-26-04-689Z/`: every request and response body, the MCP tool list, and `report.json`

content.text:
In OpenAI's hosted mode, the model found and loaded the JusPrin tools itself inside the first API response, with no extra round trip. Its search didn't use keywords: it asked for the `jusprin` namespace by name and got back all five full tool definitions. My script then had to resend those full definitions with the history on every later request. In the third turn the model called `workspace_inspect` directly, without searching again.

The whole run was 4 API calls, 19:25:31 to 19:25:44 UTC, on model `gpt-5.4`. The API reported the exact version as `gpt-5.4-2026-03-05`.

## Setup, before any API call

My script launched `jusprin-mcp` with the same arguments Claude Code uses and read two things over MCP:
- the five tool definitions;
- the server's instructions ("Inspect the live workspace, search or read process settings…").

Every request then had the same shape:
- `instructions`: the JusPrin server's instructions.
- `tools`, with two entries:
  - a `namespace` named `jusprin`, description "JusPrin 3D slicer: inspect the open project and read or change process settings.", containing all five functions, each with its full parameter schema and `defer_loading: true`;
  - `{"type": "tool_search"}`.
- `input`: the whole conversation so far. My script keeps no server-side state (`store: false`), so it resends everything.

**What the model saw before any search.** OpenAI's free token-counting endpoint measured the same first request:

| Setup | Tokens |
|---|---|
| No tools | 107 |
| The five tools, not deferred | 530 |
| The five tools deferred, plus `tool_search` | 497 |

The 497 didn't change when I padded every function description or emptied every parameter schema. It went up to 646 when I padded only the namespace description. So up front the model gets the `tool_search` tool and the namespace's name and description, but no function descriptions or schemas. Whether it also sees the five function names isn't measurable this way; names are too short to move the count reliably.

## Call 1: "what's the jusprin mcp tools do you have?" (19:25:31 → 19:25:37)

One response came back with three output items:

1. **`tool_search_call`**:
   ```json
   {"id": "tsc_028bff…", "type": "tool_search_call", "status": "completed",
    "arguments": {"paths": ["jusprin"]}, "call_id": null, "execution": "server"}
   ```
   The model asked for the namespace by path, not with a search query. `call_id` is `null` because nobody on the client side answers this call.
2. **`tool_search_output`** (`id: "tso_028bff…"`, `execution: "server"`, `call_id: null`). Its `tools` field holds the whole `jusprin` namespace: type, name and description, plus all five functions. Each function comes back with `type`, `name`, `description`, `parameters` (identical to the MCP schema), `strict`, `defer_loading: true`, and a new field, `output_schema: null`, that I hadn't sent.
3. **`message`**, with `phase: "final_answer"`: a list of the five tools with their descriptions and the preview-then-apply order from the server instructions.

Usage: 1,068 input tokens, 292 output tokens, 20 of them reasoning. I had asked for encrypted reasoning items, but none came back.

The search, its result and the answer all arrived in one HTTP response. The 1,068 input tokens are well above the 497 needed up front. My hypothesis is that they include the loaded definitions being fed to the model for its second pass inside that response; the usage figure doesn't break this down.

## Call 2: "all of them deferred?" (19:25:37 → 19:25:39)

The request's `input` resent five items:
1. the first user message;
2. the `tool_search_call`, unchanged;
3. the `tool_search_output`, unchanged, **with all five full definitions**;
4. the assistant's answer;
5. the new user message.

The `tools` array was the same as before, so every definition went over the wire twice: once in `tools` and once in the history.

The response was a single `message` with no search. The model took "deferred" to mean "waits for approval". It answered that only `settings_apply_patch` is deferred. That's a misreading of the question, which depended on our earlier Claude Code conversation, not a sign of how loading works.

Usage: 1,351 input tokens, 125 output tokens.

## Call 3: "what's on my jusprin workspace?" (19:25:39 → 19:25:42)

The `input` now had seven items: the five above, the second answer, and the new question.

The response was a single `function_call`:
```json
{"id": "fc_028bff…", "type": "function_call", "status": "completed", "arguments": "{}",
 "call_id": "REDACTED", "name": "workspace_inspect", "namespace": "jusprin"}
```
It didn't search again. The tool loaded in call 1 was still usable because its definition was in the resent `tool_search_output`. The call names the tool and its namespace in separate fields.

Usage: 1,490 input tokens, 16 output tokens.

Between calls 3 and 4, my script ran `workspace_inspect` against JusPrin over MCP.

## Call 4: sending the tool result back (19:25:42 → 19:25:44)

The `input` gained two items:
- the `function_call`, unchanged;
- a `function_call_output` with the same `call_id`, whose `output` was the MCP result as a JSON string.

The response was the final `message`: project `3x3_cali_rl_MINI`, printer preset `MyKlipper 0.4 nozzle`, filament `Generic ABS @System`, one plate, one selected object (`3x3_cali_RL.stl`, ID 97), not sliced, no unsaved changes, session ID 4, revision 17.

Usage: 1,705 input tokens, 175 output tokens.

## Things that held across all four calls

- **What the response echoes back.** Every response returned the `tools` array. The `tool_search` entry showed `description: null` and `parameters: null`, so the hosted search tool takes no configuration from the caller.
- **The tool list never changed.** The `tools` array was byte-for-byte identical in every request, with all five tools still marked deferred. Once loaded, a tool stays available because the `tool_search_output` is in the history, not because anything in `tools` changes.
- **Caching didn't happen.** Every response reported 0 cached tokens. OpenAI only caches prompts of 1,024 tokens or more, and call 1 was below that. Calls 2–4 were above it but still reported 0. I don't know why, and one run isn't enough to judge.
- **An unread field.** Each response also had a top-level `tool_usage` field. I didn't read its contents.

## Differences from Anthropic's server-side tool search

- **How the model asks.** OpenAI's model asked for a namespace path. Anthropic's docs describe a regex pattern or a keyword query.
- **What the history carries.** OpenAI's `tool_search_output` contains full definitions, and the client resends them. Anthropic's `tool_search_tool_result` carries only name references, and its API expands them on each request.
- **Round trips.** Both run the search and the answer in the same response, so neither needs an extra round trip.

All request and response bodies are in `logs/server-2026-09-15T19-25-31-841Z/` in the scratchpad, as `01-request.json` through `04-response.json`.

content.text:
I reran hosted mode with only "what's on my jusprin workspace?" in a fresh conversation. It took 2 API calls. The search and the tool call happened together inside the first response, so the extra cost of tool search here was zero round trips. Run time: 22:27:54 to 22:27:59 UTC, model `gpt-5.4-2026-03-05`.

## Call 1 (22:27:54 → 22:27:57)

**Request:** the `input` is just the user message. The `tools` array is the same as before:
- the `jusprin` namespace, with all five functions marked `defer_loading: true`;
- `{"type": "tool_search"}`.

The instructions are the JusPrin server's. From the token counts earlier, the model starts out seeing only the `tool_search` tool plus the namespace's name and description, with no function descriptions or schemas.

**Response:** three output items, in this order:
1. **`tool_search_call`**: `{"arguments": {"paths": ["jusprin"]}, "call_id": null, "execution": "server"}`. The model decided on its own to load the namespace, asking for it by name, not with a search query.
2. **`tool_search_output`**: OpenAI returned the whole namespace with all five full definitions (`type`, `name`, `description`, `parameters`, `strict`, `defer_loading`, `output_schema: null`). It loaded every tool in the namespace, not just `workspace_inspect`.
3. **`function_call`**: `{"name": "workspace_inspect", "namespace": "jusprin", "arguments": "{}", "call_id": "call_tqbegXqDBAHDowH2s0usjVVW"}`.

So OpenAI ran the search, gave the model the loaded definitions, and let it keep going until it made a call that only my script could run. Then it returned.

Usage: 1,064 input tokens, 36 output tokens, 20 of them reasoning.

**Between the calls:** my script ran `workspace_inspect` against JusPrin over MCP.

## Call 2 (22:27:57 → 22:27:59)

**Request:** `input` resent five items:
1. the user message;
2. the `tool_search_call`, unchanged;
3. the `tool_search_output`, unchanged, **including all five full definitions**;
4. the `function_call`, unchanged;
5. a `function_call_output` with the same `call_id`, holding the MCP result as a JSON string.

The `tools` array was identical to call 1.

**Response:** one `message` (`phase: "final_answer"`): project `3x3_cali_rl_MINI`, printer preset `MyKlipper 0.4 nozzle`, filament `Generic ABS @System`, one plate with one selected object (`3x3_cali_RL.stl`), not sliced, no unsaved changes.

Usage: 1,279 input tokens, 139 output tokens.

## What this means

- **Round trips:** the same as having no tool search. Search, load and call all came back in one response, followed by the usual second call to deliver the tool result.
- **What loads:** the whole namespace, all five tools, even though only one was needed. The model asked for a path, and a path loads everything under it. OpenAI's advice to keep namespaces under 10 functions follows from this.
- **What the client resends:** the full definitions, inside `tool_search_output` in the history. Anthropic's version resends only name references, and its API expands them on each request.
- **Token cost:** the real case used 1,064 input tokens, against 530 for sending the five tools without deferral. For a server this small, deferring cost more on the first call than it saved. The savings only appear with many namespaces, where just one gets loaded.
- **Caching:** 0 cached tokens on both calls. Call 2 was above OpenAI's 1,024-token minimum, so one run can't show whether caching works here.

This is one run, and the model's choice to search could vary. Logs are in `logs/server-2026-09-15T22-27-54-731Z/` in the scratchpad.

Your prediction is inverted for this setup: with tool search **off** the request was **smaller**, not larger.

| | Search off | Hosted search |
|---|---|---|
| API calls | 2 | 2 |
| Call 1 input tokens | **526** | **1,064** |
| Call 1 output | 16 (0 reasoning) | 36 (20 reasoning) |
| Call 2 input tokens | 741 | 1,279 |
| Call 2 output | 141 | 139 |
| **Total input** | **1,267** | **2,343** |
| Answer | same workspace summary | same workspace summary |

Otherwise the two runs match. Call 1 returned a `function_call` for `workspace_inspect` with `namespace: "jusprin"` and empty arguments. My script ran it over MCP. Call 2 returned the answer. The only structural difference is that the hosted run also carried `tool_search_call` and `tool_search_output` items, and those items stayed in the history for call 2.

**Why the theory doesn't hold here.** Tool search doesn't only withhold schemas, it also adds cost:
- The search machinery itself costs tokens. Measured earlier: 107 tokens with no tools at all, and 497 with the deferred namespace plus `tool_search`, of which the namespace description is a small part.
- When the model loads a namespace, it loads **every** tool in it. All five definitions arrived, the same five that would have been sent up front anyway.
- Those definitions then sit in the history and get resent on every later call, on top of the `tools` array.

So for one small server, deferring pays twice for the same schemas. All five tools cost 423 tokens up front (530 with them, 107 without), which is less than the search overhead alone.

**When your theory would hold.** With many namespaces, say ten MCP servers, always-on loading pays for all ten while tool search pays for the search plus the one namespace it opens. Anthropic's figures point at the same crossover: about 55K tokens for five servers, and their advice to use tool search past roughly 10K tokens of definitions.

If you want the crossover measured rather than argued, I can rerun with the JusPrin namespace plus a number of decoy namespaces, on and off, and show where the lines cross. Say the word and I'll run it.
